title: Capstone
tagline: Assemble everything you built into one shareable AI PM portfolio piece.
intro: Nothing new to learn this week — just assembly. You've built a scorecard, a prompt template, a guardrail file, a prototype brief, a review rubric, and a launch & monitoring plan, all for the Onboarding Packet Agent. That's not a coincidence: it's meant to read as one coherent piece of AI PM work when you put it side by side.

scenario.context: This section pulls together what you built in Weeks 1 through 6, automatically, from what's saved in your browser.
scenario.brief: Six separate exercises don't obviously add up to anything. One document that walks a single feature — the Onboarding Packet Agent — from idea, through spec, through guardrails, through prototype, through review rubric, through launch plan, reads as exactly what an AI PM does day to day, start to finish. Add a short closing reflection, then export the full portfolio piece as one Markdown file.

whatsNext.heading: What's next: the orchestrator model
whatsNext.thesis: The PM's job doesn't change — discover the right problem, define the right solution, get it built, get it adopted. What changes with AI is capacity. A PM who runs several scoped AI workstreams in parallel can sustain a depth of discovery, spec quality, and review rigor that used to take a team of analysts. The six skills you just practiced aren't isolated exercises — they're the building blocks of that model, applied one at a time. Once they're second nature, the same skills compose into running multiple scoped workstreams at once, with you as the orchestrator: scoping each one, reviewing its output, and deciding what becomes a commitment.

mapping.note: The desirability/value/viability/feasibility/usability judgment calls you made by hand are exactly what a scoring workstream needs a PM to define before it can run consistently across a large batch of ideas.
The structured prompt template you built is the seed of a scoped workstream that turns a validated idea into a build-ready spec.

Your guardrail file is a small version of the single source of truth — tool boundaries, constraints, past decisions — that every other workstream should draw from, so outputs don't drift from each other.
Going from spec to clickable outline without engineering is exactly the workstream that compresses 'is this the right direction' from weeks to hours.

mapping.week: Week 5 — Evaluating Output & the AI SDLC
mapping.note: Your rubric is the human-review checkpoint every workstream needs before its output becomes a commitment — 'agents draft, PMs decide' is the same rule you've been practicing all along.
Your readiness checklist and monitoring plan are what a launch workstream needs before anything ships broadly — and what feeds the next opportunity back into Framing, closing the loop.

whatsNext.note: A few workstreams in the fuller model — continuous competitive intelligence, syncing with a roadmap tool, and monitoring at real production scale — need enterprise tool access and data pipelines beyond a personal Claude account and synthetic data, so they're not something to practice solo end-to-end. Treat this page as a preview of where these six habits lead, not a new assignment — a fuller multi-workstream track is a natural next step once Weeks 1-6 feel automatic.

sections.heading: Closing reflection
sections.learning: The fastest way to make this stick is to run the same six steps on one real (non-sensitive, or fully within Gemini) feature idea in the next two weeks, before the habit fades — whether that's another product in the Onboarding category (E-Verify, Onboarding Forms, or WOTC), or a different Employer Services category entirely, like offboarding, ACA reporting, unemployment cost management, or ID Watchdog.

example.text: Writing the guardrail file before handing anything to an agent is the habit I'm most likely to keep — I've been skipping straight from idea to ticket, and this gives engineering something concrete to build against. I want to try it next on our ACA reporting assistant, where a bad auto-filed form is a much bigger deal than a bad onboarding packet.

sections.pitfall: Writing something generic like 'I learned a lot about AI.' A reflection with no named habit and no named place to try it is just as vague as the one-line Slack ask from Week 2 — and just as likely to never actually happen.
